conversation.content: Let's design a web search engine — think Google Search at a smaller scale. Users type a query and get ranked results. What questions do you have?

Sure. What's the scale of the web we're indexing — how many pages? What's the expected query volume? Do we need features like autocomplete, spell correction, or just basic search? And how fresh does the index need to be?
1 billion web pages indexed. 10,000 queries per second. Just basic search — no autocomplete or spell correction. Index should be refreshed weekly. Let's start.

Okay. There are three main components: crawling, indexing, and serving. The crawler discovers and downloads web pages. The indexer processes those pages and builds a searchable data structure. The serving layer takes user queries and returns ranked results. Let me walk through each.
Good structure. Start with the crawler.

The crawler starts with a seed set of URLs — maybe a few thousand known websites. It fetches each page, extracts all the links from it, and adds those links to a queue of URLs to crawl next. This is basically a BFS over the web graph. To crawl 1 billion pages in a week, that's about 1,650 pages per second. Each page fetch takes a few hundred milliseconds, so we need many concurrent crawlers — maybe 500-1,000 crawler instances running in parallel, each handling multiple concurrent HTTP requests. We need a URL frontier — the queue of URLs to crawl — with deduplication so we don't crawl the same page twice. I'd also respect robots.txt and add politeness rules — don't hammer the same domain with too many requests per second.
Good. How do you avoid crawling the same URL twice?

I'd maintain a set of already-crawled URLs. With 1 billion URLs, storing them all in memory would take a lot of space — maybe 50-100GB if each URL is 50-100 bytes. We could use a Bloom filter to check if we've seen a URL before. It's probabilistic — might have false positives — but a Bloom filter for 1 billion items with a 1% false positive rate is only about 1.2GB. False positives just mean we skip a URL we haven't actually crawled, which is acceptable. No false negatives means we never crawl the same URL twice.
Nice use of a Bloom filter. Now let's talk about indexing. How do you build a searchable index from the crawled pages?

The core data structure is an inverted index. For each word that appears in our corpus, we store a list of document IDs that contain that word — the posting list. So the entry for 'python' might point to document IDs [42, 150, 2001, ...] — all pages that contain the word 'python.' To build it, the indexer reads each crawled page, tokenizes the text — splits into words, lowercases, removes stop words — and for each token, appends the document ID to that token's posting list. Once built, a search query for 'python tutorial' finds the posting lists for 'python' and 'tutorial' and computes their intersection — documents that contain both words.
Good. How do you rank the results? If 10,000 documents contain both 'python' and 'tutorial', which ones appear first?

The simplest approach is TF-IDF — term frequency times inverse document frequency. A word that appears many times in a document (high TF) but rarely across all documents (high IDF) is a strong signal. So a page where 'python' appears 20 times ranks higher than one where it appears once, and rare terms contribute more to the score than common terms. I know Google uses something more sophisticated — PageRank I think? Where the importance of a page depends on how many other important pages link to it. But I'd probably combine TF-IDF with some simpler signals: is the query term in the title? In the URL? How fresh is the page?
Have you heard of BM25? And can you explain how PageRank actually works?

BM25 — I've seen the name but I don't know the specifics. I think it's an improvement on TF-IDF? For PageRank, I know the general idea: each page has a score based on the number and quality of pages that link to it. A link from a high-PageRank page contributes more than a link from a low-PageRank page. It's calculated iteratively — you start with equal scores and keep updating until the scores converge. But I don't know the exact formula or the details of the iterative computation.

That's okay. BM25 is essentially a saturation function over TF-IDF — it prevents very high term frequencies from dominating. PageRank is effectively a random surfer model on the web graph. Not critical for an SDE2. Let's move to the serving layer. How do you serve queries at 10K QPS?

The inverted index for 1 billion documents is too large for a single machine. I'd shard it — partition the index across multiple servers. One approach is document-based sharding: each shard holds the full index for a subset of documents. When a query comes in, we fan out to all shards in parallel, each shard returns its top-K results, and we merge the results into a final top-K. The query coordinator handles the fan-out and merge. With, say, 100 shards, each holds about 10 million documents — manageable for a single machine's memory.
What about the alternative — term-based sharding? What are the trade-offs?

Term-based sharding puts all posting lists for words starting with 'a' on one set of servers, 'b' on another, and so on. The advantage is that a single-term query only hits one shard. The disadvantage is that multi-term queries still need to hit multiple shards, and you have to transfer and intersect posting lists across the network. Also, some terms are way more popular than others, leading to hot shards. Document-based sharding is more uniform and simpler to manage, which is why I'd go with it.
Good trade-off analysis. What about caching at the query serving layer?

Query caching is huge for search. Many queries are repeated — 'weather,' 'facebook,' 'amazon' probably make up a significant percentage of all searches. I'd cache the full result set for popular queries in Redis or Memcached. The cache key is the normalized query string. Since our index refreshes weekly, cache TTL can be long — hours or even until the next index rebuild. A query cache with even a 30% hit rate would dramatically reduce load on the index servers.
What happens when you rebuild the index weekly? How do you cut over without downtime?

I'd build the new index offline on a separate set of servers. Once the new index is fully built and verified — check document counts, run test queries — I'd do a blue-green deployment. Route traffic to the new index servers, keep the old ones as a fallback. If the new index has issues, we can roll back by pointing traffic back to the old servers. The cache gets invalidated during the cutover since the result rankings may have changed.
Good. Anything else you'd want to add?

I'd add a snippet generation service that extracts relevant text passages from the matching documents to show in search results. Also, analytics to track query latency, click-through rates, and zero-result queries — the last one helps identify gaps in the index. And a simple spam detection layer to demote SEO-manipulated pages.
Good discussion for an SDE2. You understand the fundamentals of crawling and inverted indexes well. Deeper knowledge of ranking algorithms like BM25 and PageRank would strengthen your design. Thanks.

strengths: Clear explanation of inverted index construction and query intersection
Good use of Bloom filter for URL deduplication with concrete sizing math
Reasonable trade-off analysis between document-based and term-based sharding
weaknesses: Does not know BM25 — the standard relevance ranking algorithm used by all major search engines
PageRank understanding is vague — only knows the general concept
No discussion of query parsing, stemming, or language processing
Did not cover API design or query latency requirements
